power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Adolescent mental health problems have increased globally, yet existing frameworks struggle to explain how multilevel social conditions translate into enduring psychological vulnerability.

Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory and its later bioecological model have provided a foundational lens for understanding contextual influences on development, but applications of the theory remain largely descriptive and insufficiently integrated with contemporary evidence on biological embedding, institutional regulation, and historical change.

This narrative review proposes an Extended, Process-Oriented Ecological Framework for Adolescent Mental Health (EEF-AMH) that reconceptualizes ecological systems as dynamically interconnected processes through which stress is produced, regulated, translated, and accumulated across development.

Synthesizing longitudinal studies, meta-analyses, and interdisciplinary research, the framework integrates individual biological sensitivity, relational dynamics within families and peer groups, institutional and digital regulation, structural inequality, and temporal processes.
Rather than cataloguing risk factors at discrete ecological levels, the EEF-AMH emphasizes mechanisms linking distal macrosocial conditions to proximal emotional experiences and biological embedding.
The chronosystem is foregrounded as an active explanatory dimension, highlighting how timing, duration, and cumulative exposure shape mental health trajectories and cohort-level trends.

By shifting ecological theory from static context to dynamic process, the EEF-AMH provides a contemporary explanatory model for adolescent mental health disparities and offers a conceptual foundation for multilevel prevention, intervention, and policy approaches.

Adolescent mental health problems have become a major public health concern worldwide, with rising prevalence of depression, anxiety, self-harm, and stress-related disorders across diverse sociocultural contexts (World Health Organization, 2025).
text.formatted: Adolescent mental health problems have become a major public health concern worldwide, with rising prevalence of depression, anxiety, self-harm, and stress-related disorders across diverse sociocultural contexts <ref type="bibr">(World Health Organization, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These difficulties do not arise from isolated causes but reflect the interplay of individual vulnerabilities and multilayered environmental conditions.

Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory has long provided a foundational framework for understanding such complexity, conceptualizing development as embedded within nested systems ranging from immediate interpersonal relationships to broader sociocultural and historical contexts (Bronfenbrenner, 1979).
text.formatted: Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory has long provided a foundational framework for understanding such complexity, conceptualizing development as embedded within nested systems ranging from immediate interpersonal relationships to broader sociocultural and historical contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Bronfenbrenner, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: Its emphasis on contextual embeddedness and person-environment interaction has profoundly shaped developmental and mental health research.
Despite its enduring influence, the original ecological systems framework faces important limitations when applied to contemporary adolescent mental health.

First, Bronfenbrenner's early formulations offered limited integration of biological and dispositional processes, such as genetic vulnerability, neurodevelopmental sensitivity, and stress-related biological embedding, which are now central to developmental psychopathology.
Second, the theory predates the emergence of digital environments that have become pervasive contexts of social interaction, identity formation, and exposure to stress in adolescence.

Third, ecological systems were largely conceptualized as structurally nested but analytically discrete, offering limited guidance on how stressors, meanings, and regulatory forces are transmitted and transformed across systems over time.

As a result, traditional applications of ecological theory often describe where risk factors reside rather than explaining how multilevel risks dynamically interact to shape mental health trajectories.
These limitations apply most directly to the early ecological systems model (Bronfenbrenner, 1979).
text.formatted: These limitations apply most directly to the early ecological systems model <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Bronfenbrenner, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: In later work, Bronfenbrenner reformulated the theory as the bioecological model and its Process-Person-Context-Time (PPCT) design (Bronfenbrenner & Ceci, 1994; Bronfenbrenner & Morris, 2006).

text.text: In this mature form, proximal processes, defined as regular and enduring interactions between the developing person and the immediate environment, are the primary engines of development.

Their form and power vary with characteristics of the person, with the immediate and more remote context, and with time, which is examined at the levels of microtime, mesotime, and macrotime (Bronfenbrenner & Morris, 2006).

text.text: The model also proposed that genetic potentials are actualized through proximal processes (Bronfenbrenner & Ceci, 1994).

text.text: The bioecological model therefore already treats development as a process and accounts for to biological dispositions and to historical time.

Applications of the theory have nevertheless relied largely on the early nested-systems model, and a review of 25 studies citing the theory found that only four used its mature PPCT form (Tudge et al., 2009).

text.text: The present framework builds on the bioecological model rather than on the early model alone, and it addresses three questions that the bioecological model leaves open for adolescent mental health.

The first is how distal structures in the macrosystem and exosystem reach proximal processes, since the bioecological model treats the wider context mainly as a set of conditions that moderate those processes.
The second is how adversity becomes biologically embedded.

The bioecological model describes how genetic potentials are realized under supportive proximal processes and characterizes the person in terms of dispositions, resources, and demands, but it does not specify how chronic stress becomes linked to changes in stress physiology, gene expression, or epigenetic regulation.
The third is how institutions that did not exist when the theory was formulated, such as digital platforms and their governance, shape the conditions under which proximal processes occur.
Recent advances underscore the need for a process-oriented extension of ecological theory.

Research in genetics, epigenetics, and psychobiology demonstrates that social and structural stressors may become biologically embedded, with associated changes in stress physiology and emotional regulation that may confer long-term vulnerability (Ochi & Dwivedi, 2023; Tollenaar et al., 2025).

text.text: At the same time, institutional and regulatory forces-such as educational systems, digital platforms, economic policies, and cultural norms-actively shape how risks are distributed, perceived, and managed within families, schools, and peer contexts.

These developments suggest that adolescent mental health risk emerges not simply from exposure within ecological levels, but from the transmission, amplification, and accumulation of stress across systems and across time (Raviv et al., 2010).

text.text: This article adopts a theory-extending narrative review approach to synthesize and integrate evidence on adolescent mental health within an ecological framework.

Rather than aiming to provide an exhaustive or systematic summary of all available studies, the review selectively draws on representative empirical and theoretical work to clarify mechanisms linking multilevel ecological stressors to mental health outcomes across development.

Relevant literature was identified through targeted searches of major academic databases, including PsycINFO, PubMed, and Web of Science, using combinations of keywords related to adolescent mental health, ecological systems, stress exposure, biological embedding, family and peer processes, institutional contexts, and social inequality.

Priority was given to longitudinal studies, meta-analyses, and highly cited theoretical contributions, as these designs are best suited to informing developmental processes and cross-level interactions.
Additional sources were identified through reference tracing of key articles.
The purpose of this review is not to quantify effect sizes or establish causal estimates, but to advance conceptual understanding by integrating findings across disciplines and levels of analysis.

Consistent with theory-extending narrative reviews, evidence is used illustratively to support the proposed Extended, Process-Oriented Ecological Framework for Adolescent Mental Health (EEF-AMH), highlighting central mechanisms rather than cataloguing all potential correlates of adolescent mental health.

The literature reviewed is therefore illustrative rather than exhaustive, and the EEF-AMH is offered as a conceptual synthesis that generates testable propositions, not as a formally validated theoretical model.
Accordingly, terms such as production, regulation, translation, embedding, and accumulation describe the functional roles that the framework proposes for each ecological level.
They are not claims that each pathway has been causally established, and much of the supporting evidence remains observational.
The EEF-AMH is organized around five processes.

Structural risk production operates in the macrosystem, institutional regulation in the exosystem, relational translation in the microsystem, biological embedding at the person level, and temporal accumulation in the chronosystem.
These processes were identified in three steps.
First, they were derived theoretically.

For each ecological level, we asked what function that level serves in the transmission of stress to the adolescent and anchored the answer in an established theory that already describes this function.

Structural risk production draws on fundamental cause theory, which holds that social conditions affect health by shaping access to resources that protect against many risks at once (Link & Phelan, 1995).

text.text: Institutional regulation draws on social determinants of health frameworks, which distinguish structural determinants from the intermediary conditions, including health systems, through which they act (Solar & Irwin, 2010).

text.text: Relational translation draws on the Family Stress Model, which specifies pathways from economic pressure to caregiver distress and parenting (Conger et al., 1992), and on the bioecological emphasis on proximal processes (Bronfenbrenner & Morris, 2006).

text.text: Second, each process was retained only when longitudinal or meta-analytic evidence linked it to adolescent mental health outcomes.
This evidence is reviewed in the sections that follow.
Third, the set was chosen because it brings together disciplines that usually address adolescent mental health separately.

Social epidemiology speaks mainly to risk production, health services and policy research to institutional regulation, family and developmental psychology to relational translation, psychobiology to biological embedding, and life course research to accumulation.
Organizing these literatures around a sequence of processes allows them to be read as parts of one account rather than as parallel lists of correlates.

The sections that follow describe each level in turn, beginning with the person and moving outward to the macrosystem and the chronosystem.

Within an extended ecological perspective, individual-level vulnerability does not represent an isolated source of risk but rather the primary site at which multilevel stressors converge and become biologically embedded (Danese & McEwen, 2012).

text.text: Contemporary developmental psychopathology emphasizes that adolescents' emotional reactivity, genetic liability, and physiological stress responses function as interfaces between ecological exposures and mental health outcomes.

From this view, the person level is not merely one ecological layer among others, but the level at which distal social and structural stressors are translated into enduring neurobiological and psychological vulnerability (Cicchetti & Rogosch, 2002).

text.text: A central mechanism linking ecological stress to adolescent mental health is heightened emotional reactivity.

Adolescents characterized by elevated negative emotionality or affective sensitivity tend to exhibit stronger and more prolonged responses to stressors, rendering them particularly susceptible to anxiety and depressive symptoms (Dollar et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Adolescents characterized by elevated negative emotionality or affective sensitivity tend to exhibit stronger and more prolonged responses to stressors, rendering them particularly susceptible to anxiety and depressive symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Dollar et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, emotional reactivity does not operate independently of context.

Longitudinal research indicates that high-reactivity youth are disproportionately affected by family conflict, peer adversity, and other environmental stressors, consistent with diathesis-stress and differential susceptibility models (Rabinowitz et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Longitudinal research indicates that high-reactivity youth are disproportionately affected by family conflict, peer adversity, and other environmental stressors, consistent with diathesis-stress and differential susceptibility models <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">(Rabinowitz et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Emotional reactivity thus functions as a stress amplifier, magnifying the psychological impact of exposures arising in proximal and distal ecological systems.
Genetic liability further shapes adolescents' sensitivity to environmental stress.

Advances in molecular genetics demonstrate that polygenic risk scores (PRS) for depression and related disorders predict not only baseline symptom severity but also steeper symptom trajectories across adolescence (Kwong et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Advances in molecular genetics demonstrate that polygenic risk scores (PRS) for depression and related disorders predict not only baseline symptom severity but also steeper symptom trajectories across adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Kwong et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, genetic vulnerability interacts with environmental exposure rather than determining outcomes on its own.

Adolescents with elevated genetic risk appear particularly vulnerable in contexts characterized by chronic stress, socioeconomic disadvantage, or relational instability, underscoring how macrosystem and microsystem stressors may differentially affect youth depending on underlying biological sensitivity (Rutter et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Adolescents with elevated genetic risk appear particularly vulnerable in contexts characterized by chronic stress, socioeconomic disadvantage, or relational instability, underscoring how macrosystem and microsystem stressors may differentially affect youth depending on underlying biological sensitivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">(Rutter et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond inherited vulnerability, emerging evidence highlights biological embedding as a key process through which ecological stress becomes developmentally consequential.
Exposure to adversity-particularly when chronic or occurring during sensitive developmental windowshas been linked to alterations in stress physiology, immune functioning, and cellular aging.

Epigenetic mechanisms, including changes in DNA methylation and telomere length, provide a plausible pathway linking experiences such as family conflict, abuse, or persistent socioeconomic strain to long-term differences in emotional regulation and mental health (Ochi & Dwivedi, 2023; Tollenaar et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Epigenetic mechanisms, including changes in DNA methylation and telomere length, provide a plausible pathway linking experiences such as family conflict, abuse, or persistent socioeconomic strain to long-term differences in emotional regulation and mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Ochi & Dwivedi, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Tollenaar et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that ecological stressors do not merely co-occur with adolescent mental health problems but may become biologically instantiated, shaping stress responsivity and vulnerability over time.
Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) represent one of the most robust and welldocumented sources of biologically embedding stress.

Exposure to abuse, neglect, household dysfunction, and related adversities shows strong dose-response associations with depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress symptoms during adolescence (Elmore & Crouch, 2020; Humphreys et al., 2020; Lam et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Exposure to abuse, neglect, household dysfunction, and related adversities shows strong dose-response associations with depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress symptoms during adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Elmore & Crouch, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Humphreys et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Lam et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, ACEs rarely occur in isolation (Dong et al., 2004); they are disproportionately concentrated among youth exposed to broader structural disadvantages, including poverty, housing instability, and community violence (Walsh et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Importantly, ACEs rarely occur in isolation <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Dong et al., 2004)</ref>; they are disproportionately concentrated among youth exposed to broader structural disadvantages, including poverty, housing instability, and community violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">(Walsh et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: From an ecological perspective, ACEs thus exemplify how macrosystem and exosystem conditions permeate the family microsystem and ultimately manifest as individual-level psychopathology.
Biological embedding processes are further compounded by lifestyle-related stressors that are themselves shaped by ecological context.
Sleep disruption, physical inactivity, and nutritional insufficiency are common among adolescents facing chronic stress and institutional constraint.

Experimental and longitudinal evidence demonstrates that insufficient or irregular sleep heightens emotional reactivity and undermines mood regulation (Blacher et al., 2024; Booth et al., 2021; Marino et al., 2021), while physical inactivity and poor nutrition exacerbate stress sensitivity and depressive symptoms (Fu et al., 2025; Hou et al., 2025; Fiani et al., 2024; Kirolos et al., 2022).

text.text: These factors are not merely individual behaviors but reflect the downstream consequences of school demands, neighborhood safety, socioeconomic resources, and digital engagement patterns (Alosaimi et al., 2023).
text.formatted: These factors are not merely individual behaviors but reflect the downstream consequences of school demands, neighborhood safety, socioeconomic resources, and digital engagement patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alosaimi et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, lifestyle disruptions may be understood as secondary embedding pathways through which ecological stress amplifies vulnerability at the person level.
Chronic physical health conditions provide an additional illustration of stress embedding across systems.

Adolescents managing long-term illnesses face persistent physiological stress, medical uncertainty, and disruptions to normative social participation, all of which elevate risk for depression and anxiety (Barker et al., 2019; Stein, 2022).
text.formatted: Adolescents managing long-term illnesses face persistent physiological stress, medical uncertainty, and disruptions to normative social participation, all of which elevate risk for depression and anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Barker et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Stein, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These burdens are often intensified by socioeconomic disadvantage and limited access to healthcare, highlighting cross-system interactions between biological vulnerability, family resources, and institutional support (Kirkbride et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These burdens are often intensified by socioeconomic disadvantage and limited access to healthcare, highlighting cross-system interactions between biological vulnerability, family resources, and institutional support <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Kirkbride et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In this sense, chronic illness operates not only as an individual health factor but as an ecologically situated stressor that links biological, relational, and structural domains.

Taken together, evidence from genetics, psychobiology, and developmental research underscores that adolescent mental health risk emerges through processes of stress amplification and biological embedding, rather than through isolated individual traits.

Emotional reactivity, genetic liability, and physiological dysregulation constitute key pathways through which ecological adversity becomes internalized, shaping trajectories of anxiety and depression across adolescence.

Understanding these processes is essential for integrating individual-level vulnerability within a broader ecological framework and for identifying points of intervention that interrupt the translation of contextual stress into enduring mental health risk.

Within the extended ecological framework, the microsystem occupies a pivotal position as the primary context in which broader social, economic, and institutional stressors are translated into adolescents' daily emotional experiences.

Families, peer groups, and schools do not merely coexist alongside macrosystem and exosystem forces; rather, they function as relational filters that shape how distal pressures are interpreted, enacted, and emotionally internalized.
Consequently, microsystem processes are likely to play a central role in whether ecological stressors are buffered or amplified in adolescents' mental health trajectories.
Figure 1 marks this role with the label buffer/amplify on the arrow that leaves the microsystem.

text.text: Family relationships represent the core microsystem through which stress is most consistently transmitted.

A substantial body of longitudinal and meta-analytic evidence demonstrates that chronic interparental conflict, psychologically controlling or harsh parenting, and persistent parent-adolescent discord are robust predictors of adolescent depression, anxiety, and behavioral difficulties (Evans et al., 2008; Kitzmann et al., 2003; McLeod et al., 2007; Norman et al., 2012; Rhoades, 2008).
text.formatted: A substantial body of longitudinal and meta-analytic evidence demonstrates that chronic interparental conflict, psychologically controlling or harsh parenting, and persistent parent-adolescent discord are robust predictors of adolescent depression, anxiety, and behavioral difficulties <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Evans et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Kitzmann et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">McLeod et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Norman et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Rhoades, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, these relational patterns rarely arise in isolation.

Economic strain, parental psychopathology, housing instability, and exposure to discrimination-factors rooted in the macrosystem and exosystem-frequently disrupt caregivers' emotional availability and regulatory capacity.

Consistent with the Family Stress Model, such upstream stressors erode parenting quality, increase interparental hostility, and create emotionally unpredictable home environments, thereby transforming structural disadvantage into proximal relational risk (Conger et al., 1992; Yoshikawa et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Consistent with the Family Stress Model, such upstream stressors erode parenting quality, increase interparental hostility, and create emotionally unpredictable home environments, thereby transforming structural disadvantage into proximal relational risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Conger et al., 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">Yoshikawa et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: From a process-oriented perspective, the psychological impact of family adversity is best understood through its effects on emotional climate and attachment-related security.
Persistent exposure to hostile or inconsistent caregiving undermines adolescents' sense of safety and predictability, impairing emotion regulation and stress recovery (Repetti et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Persistent exposure to hostile or inconsistent caregiving undermines adolescents' sense of safety and predictability, impairing emotion regulation and stress recovery <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Repetti et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Family Systems Theory further elucidates how stress proliferates within the microsystem (Bowen, 1978; Kerr & Bowen, 1988).
text.formatted: Family Systems Theory further elucidates how stress proliferates within the microsystem <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Bowen, 1978;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Kerr & Bowen, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: Mechanisms such as triangulation-where adolescents are drawn into unresolved interparental conflict (Fosco & Grych, 2008)-and boundary disturbances, including enmeshment or disengagement (Coe et al., 2018; van Eickels et al., 2022), represent systemic attempts to manage stress that inadvertently increase youth vulnerability.

text.text: These relational configurations compromise autonomy development while intensifying emotional burden, creating fertile conditions for internalising symptoms during adolescence.
Attachment processes provide an additional explanatory bridge linking relational dynamics to mental health outcomes (Costa et al., 2022; Spangler & Zimmermann, 1999; Wang et al., 2024).

text.text: Adolescents exposed to chronic conflict or emotionally unavailable caregiving are more likely to develop insecure internal working models, characterized by heightened threat sensitivity, reduced trust in support figures, and maladaptive emotion regulation strategies (Spruit et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Adolescents exposed to chronic conflict or emotionally unavailable caregiving are more likely to develop insecure internal working models, characterized by heightened threat sensitivity, reduced trust in support figures, and maladaptive emotion regulation strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">(Spruit et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Such patterns not only increase susceptibility to depression and anxiety but also interact with individual-level vulnerabilities, including heightened emotional reactivity and biological stress sensitivity (Brumariu, 2015).
text.formatted: Such patterns not only increase susceptibility to depression and anxiety but also interact with individual-level vulnerabilities, including heightened emotional reactivity and biological stress sensitivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Brumariu, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In this way, the microsystem operates as a key site where ecological stressors intersect with personal predispositions, shaping both psychological and physiological pathways of risk.

Peer relationships constitute a parallel microsystem through which stress is translated into emotional experience, particularly during adolescence when sensitivity to social evaluation and belonging intensifies.

Peer victimization, rejection, and chronic loneliness reliably predict depressive symptoms, anxiety, self-harm, and suicidality (Kasturiratna et al., 2025; Moore et al., 2017; van Geel et al., 2014; Ye et al., 2023).

text.text: These experiences may matter not only as discrete events but also through their links to adolescents' perceptions of social worth and safety.
Repeated exposure to rejection or humiliation fosters shame, social threat vigilance, and withdrawal, thereby reinforcing internalising trajectories (Irwin et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Repeated exposure to rejection or humiliation fosters shame, social threat vigilance, and withdrawal, thereby reinforcing internalising trajectories <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Irwin et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, peer adversity is often patterned by broader ecological forces, including school climate, neighborhood safety, digital platform design, and structural stigma, underscoring the embeddedness of peer stress within larger systems (Hong & Espelage, 2012; Patel & Quan-Haase, 2024).
text.formatted: Notably, peer adversity is often patterned by broader ecological forces, including school climate, neighborhood safety, digital platform design, and structural stigma, underscoring the embeddedness of peer stress within larger systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Hong & Espelage, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Patel & Quan-Haase, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Schools function as an additional microsystem in which relational processes either buffer or exacerbate stress.

School climates characterized by fairness, inclusion, and supportive teacher-student relationships are consistently associated with lower levels of depression and anxiety, even among youth facing adversity in other domains (Raniti et al., 2022).
text.formatted: School climates characterized by fairness, inclusion, and supportive teacher-student relationships are consistently associated with lower levels of depression and anxiety, even among youth facing adversity in other domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Raniti et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, punitive disciplinary practices, academic pressure, and environments perceived as unsafe or exclusionary can amplify stress and undermine belonging (So et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Conversely, punitive disciplinary practices, academic pressure, and environments perceived as unsafe or exclusionary can amplify stress and undermine belonging <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">(So et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, schools often reflect and reproduce macrosystem inequalities, such as differential resource allocation or discriminatory practices, which are subsequently enacted through daily interpersonal interactions within classrooms and peer groups.
Across family, peer, and school contexts, the microsystem thus operates as a translational nexus in the ecological system.

Structural stressors originating in the macrosystem and exosystem-such as poverty, discrimination, policy environments, and digital regulation-are rendered psychologically meaningful through everyday relational exchanges.
When these exchanges are characterized by warmth, stability, and inclusion, microsystems can buffer adolescents from broader adversity.
When marked by conflict, rejection, or unpredictability, they amplify stress exposure and accelerate processes of emotional dysregulation and biological embedding.
In sum, microsystem processes are not merely proximal correlates of adolescent mental health but appear to be primary pathways through which ecological risk is enacted in daily life.
By shaping emotional climate, attachment security, and social belonging, families, peers, and schools help shape whether broader ecological pressures are transformed into resilience or vulnerability.

Understanding the microsystem as a site of relational translation is therefore essential for explaining how multilevel stressors converge to influence adolescent mental health and for identifying intervention targets capable of disrupting the transmission of risk across ecological systems.

Within an extended ecological framework, the exosystem encompasses the institutional, organizational, and infrastructural contexts that shape adolescents' lives indirectly by regulating access to resources, opportunities, and protection.

Although adolescents may not engage directly with exosystem actors-such as healthcare systems, educational administrations, labor markets, or digital platform governance-the policies and practices embedded within these systems profoundly influence the functioning of families, schools, and peer networks.
From a processoriented perspective, the exosystem operates as a regulatory layer that influences whether microsystems are equipped to buffer stress or instead become sites of risk amplification.
In Figure 1, this role is shown as institutional regulation of the resources that reach families, schools, and peer networks.

text.text: A central exosystem mechanism is access to mental health and social support services.

Communities characterized by limited availability of affordable, youth-sensitive mental health care often leave emerging psychological difficulties unaddressed, allowing distress to escalate into more severe disorders (Graves et al., 2024; Meng & Wiznitzer, 2024; Radez et al., 2021).

text.text: Geographic disparities in service provision, long waiting times, financial barriers, and stigmarelated obstacles disproportionately affect adolescents from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds (Radez et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Geographic disparities in service provision, long waiting times, financial barriers, and stigmarelated obstacles disproportionately affect adolescents from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Radez et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In such contexts, families and schools are expected to manage complex emotional and behavioral needs with insufficient professional support, increasing relational strain and undermining microsystem stability (Angold et al., 1998).
text.formatted: In such contexts, families and schools are expected to manage complex emotional and behavioral needs with insufficient professional support, increasing relational strain and undermining microsystem stability <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Angold et al., 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, robust service infrastructures-such as school-based counseling, community youth programs, and integrated care models-can reduce caregiver burden, enhance early detection, and interrupt the progression of distress before it becomes entrenched (Haft et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Conversely, robust service infrastructures-such as school-based counseling, community youth programs, and integrated care models-can reduce caregiver burden, enhance early detection, and interrupt the progression of distress before it becomes entrenched <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Haft et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond healthcare access, institutional policies and practices shape adolescents' daily stress exposure.
Educational systems, for example, regulate academic pressure, disciplinary practices, and inclusion through formal policies that are enacted within classrooms.

Punitive disciplinary regimes, exclusionary practices, or high-stakes evaluation systems may intensify stress, foster alienation, and exacerbate peer conflict, particularly among marginalized youth (So et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Punitive disciplinary regimes, exclusionary practices, or high-stakes evaluation systems may intensify stress, foster alienation, and exacerbate peer conflict, particularly among marginalized youth <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">(So et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, restorative approaches, inclusive policies, and adequate student support services can foster psychological safety and belonging, enabling schools to function as protective microsystems even in the presence of external adversity (Raniti et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In contrast, restorative approaches, inclusive policies, and adequate student support services can foster psychological safety and belonging, enabling schools to function as protective microsystems even in the presence of external adversity <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Raniti et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These patterns illustrate how exosystem-level governance structures may be translated into relational climates that are closely linked to adolescent mental health.
Digital platforms constitute an increasingly salient exosystem context.

Adolescents' online experiences are not simply the product of individual choices but are shaped by platform architectures, algorithmic recommendation systems, content moderation practices, and data governance policies (Chhabra et al., 2025; Costello et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Adolescents' online experiences are not simply the product of individual choices but are shaped by platform architectures, algorithmic recommendation systems, content moderation practices, and data governance policies <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Chhabra et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Costello et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Weak regulation of youthoriented digital environments permits the proliferation of harmful content, including cyberbullying, appearance-based comparison, self-harm material, and misinformation (Lee et al., 2025a; Nagata et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Weak regulation of youthoriented digital environments permits the proliferation of harmful content, including cyberbullying, appearance-based comparison, self-harm material, and misinformation <ref type="bibr">(Lee et al., 2025a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Nagata et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These exposures can destabilize peer relationships, intensify social evaluation, and disrupt sleep and emotional regulation within the microsystem.

Importantly, the psychological risks associated with digital media are not inherent to technology itself but reflect regulatory choices embedded within exosystem structures (National Scientific Council on Adolescence, 2022; Odgers & Jensen, 2020).
text.formatted: Importantly, the psychological risks associated with digital media are not inherent to technology itself but reflect regulatory choices embedded within exosystem structures (National Scientific Council on Adolescence, 2022; <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Odgers & Jensen, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Platform designs that prioritize engagement over well-being may therefore function as institutional stressors, while age-appropriate design codes and content safeguards represent potential buffering mechanisms (Chhabra et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Platform designs that prioritize engagement over well-being may therefore function as institutional stressors, while age-appropriate design codes and content safeguards represent potential buffering mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Chhabra et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Community infrastructure further shapes adolescents' exposure to risk and protection.

Access to safe recreational spaces, youth clubs, and extracurricular opportunities provides structured environments for social connection, stress relief, and identity exploration (Boelens et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Access to safe recreational spaces, youth clubs, and extracurricular opportunities provides structured environments for social connection, stress relief, and identity exploration <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Boelens et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In under-resourced neighborhoods, the absence of such spaces may increase reliance on unsupervised or online environments, heightening exposure to peer risk and social isolation (Gordon-Larsen et al., 2006).
text.formatted: In under-resourced neighborhoods, the absence of such spaces may increase reliance on unsupervised or online environments, heightening exposure to peer risk and social isolation <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Gordon-Larsen et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, transportation systems, housing stability, and neighborhood safety indirectly influence family stress levels (Hatem et al., 2020) and adolescents' autonomy (Lee et al., 2025b), illustrating how exosystem conditions may extend into microsystem functioning.
text.formatted: Similarly, transportation systems, housing stability, and neighborhood safety indirectly influence family stress levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Hatem et al., 2020</ref>) and adolescents' autonomy <ref type="bibr">(Lee et al., 2025b)</ref>, illustrating how exosystem conditions may extend into microsystem functioning.

text.text: Crucially, exosystem influences are not evenly distributed.

Structural inequalities ensure that disadvantaged communities are more likely to experience underfunded schools, limited mental health services, and weaker regulatory protections, thereby compounding stress across ecological levels.
These disparities mean that adolescents facing the greatest need for buffering support are often embedded within the least protective exosystem contexts.
As a result, the exosystem plays a central role in reproducing or mitigating mental health inequalities by shaping the conditions under which microsystems operate.
In summary, the exosystem functions as a regulatory and distributive engine within the ecological system, organizing how resources, protections, and risks are allocated across populations.

By setting the institutional conditions that govern family functioning, school climate, peer interaction, and digital engagement, exosystem processes may influence whether broader ecological stressors are absorbed, transformed, or amplified before reaching the individual.

Recognizing the exosystem as an active mechanism of regulation-rather than a passive backdrop-clarifies how policy, institutional design, and infrastructure constitute critical leverage points for improving adolescent mental health outcomes.

Within the extended ecological framework, the macrosystem represents the broad social, economic, cultural, and political structures that shape the distribution of risk and protection across populations.

Unlike proximal systems that operate through direct interaction, the macrosystem is thought to operate by defining the normative, material, and regulatory conditions under which adolescents and their families live.

From a process-oriented perspective, the macrosystem functions as a risk-producing system, generating patterned exposure to stressors that are subsequently transmitted through institutional and relational pathways.
In Figure 1, the macrosystem appears at the top of the cascade as the level of structural risk production.
text.formatted: In Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, the macrosystem appears at the top of the cascade as the level of structural risk production.

text.text: Socioeconomic inequality constitutes one of the most robust macrosystem determinants of adolescent mental health.

Extensive epidemiological evidence demonstrates that adolescents growing up in poverty or in highly unequal societies face substantially elevated risks of depression, anxiety, behavioral problems, and self-harm (Kirkbride et al., 2024; McLaughlin et al., 2012; Reiss, 2013).
text.formatted: Extensive epidemiological evidence demonstrates that adolescents growing up in poverty or in highly unequal societies face substantially elevated risks of depression, anxiety, behavioral problems, and self-harm <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Kirkbride et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">McLaughlin et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Reiss, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, these associations are not well explained by individual deficits and are better understood as reflecting structural conditions that concentrate adversitysuch as housing instability, food insecurity, under-resourced schools, and neighborhood violence -among disadvantaged groups.

Persistent exposure to socioeconomic disadvantage appears particularly harmful, as chronic material insecurity and uncertainty are thought to generate sustained stress that may spread through family functioning, school experiences, and biological stress systems.
From an ecological perspective, poverty operates not as a distal correlate but as a foundational macrosystem force that shapes risk across all lower levels.

Beyond material deprivation, structural discrimination and stigma constitute critical macrosystem processes that disproportionately affect marginalized adolescents (Ahmad et al., 2022; Dotsikas et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Beyond material deprivation, structural discrimination and stigma constitute critical macrosystem processes that disproportionately affect marginalized adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ahmad et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Dotsikas et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Systems of racism, heteronormativity, and other forms of institutionalized bias allocate resources and opportunities along social group lines, exposing some youth to chronic stress while shielding others.

Adolescents who belong to stigmatized groups often encounter discrimination not only through interpersonal encounters but also through unequal policies and exclusionary practices (Benner et al., 2018; Russell & Fish, 2016; Priest et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Adolescents who belong to stigmatized groups often encounter discrimination not only through interpersonal encounters but also through unequal policies and exclusionary practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Benner et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Russell & Fish, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Priest et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These macrosystem conditions give rise to minority stress, characterized by heightened vigilance, expectations of rejection, and internalized stigma, which are strongly linked to depression, anxiety, and suicidality (Black et al., 2023; Meyer, 2003).
text.formatted: These macrosystem conditions give rise to minority stress, characterized by heightened vigilance, expectations of rejection, and internalized stigma, which are strongly linked to depression, anxiety, and suicidality <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Black et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Meyer, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, evidence suggests that observed mental health disparities reflect, in large part, differential exposure to structural stressors rather than inherent group differences, underscoring the central role of macrosystem forces in producing inequality (Kirkbride et al., 2024).

text.text: Cultural norms and value systems further shape adolescent mental health by regulating expectations, identities, and acceptable forms of distress.

Norms surrounding academic achievement, emotional expression, gender roles, and body ideals can function as chronic sources of pressure during adolescence, a developmental period marked by heightened sensitivity to evaluation and belonging.
In contexts where success is narrowly defined or failure is stigmatized, adolescents may experience pervasive performance anxiety, shame, and fear of social devaluation.
Similarly, rigid gender norms that discourage emotional disclosure among boys or emphasize appearance among girls are associated with increased internalizing symptoms and diminished self-worth.

These cultural pressures are amplified through media ecosystems that circulate idealized images and narratives, reinforcing normative standards that many adolescents perceive as unattainable (Fardouly & Vartanian, 2016; Mokhwelepa & Sumbane, 2025; Steare et al., 2023).
text.formatted: These cultural pressures are amplified through media ecosystems that circulate idealized images and narratives, reinforcing normative standards that many adolescents perceive as unattainable <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Fardouly & Vartanian, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Mokhwelepa & Sumbane, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Steare et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Mass media and digital culture constitute a powerful macrosystem channel through which norms are disseminated and intensified.

Algorithmically curated media environments can amplify appearance-based comparison, fear-inducing content, and polarized discourse, shaping adolescents' perceptions of self and society (Anand et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Algorithmically curated media environments can amplify appearance-based comparison, fear-inducing content, and polarized discourse, shaping adolescents' perceptions of self and society <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Anand et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: While digital platforms are experienced at the individual and peer levels, the values embedded within these systems-such as prioritizing engagement, visibility, and competition-reflect macrosystem logics that influence psychological well-being at scale.

Importantly, cultural and media environments are not inherently harmful; shifts toward inclusive representation, body positivity, and mental health awareness demonstrate that macrosystem norms can also foster resilience and validation when deliberately shaped (Evans-Lacko et al., 2014; Nelson et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Importantly, cultural and media environments are not inherently harmful; shifts toward inclusive representation, body positivity, and mental health awareness demonstrate that macrosystem norms can also foster resilience and validation when deliberately shaped <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Evans-Lacko et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Nelson et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Public policy represents another critical macrosystem lever influencing adolescent mental health.

Laws and policies governing education, healthcare, housing, labor, and digital regulation establish the structural conditions under which stressors are generated or mitigated (Kirkbride et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Laws and policies governing education, healthcare, housing, labor, and digital regulation establish the structural conditions under which stressors are generated or mitigated <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Kirkbride et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For example, inequitable school funding, limited access to mental health care, or weak protections against discrimination systematically increase stress exposure for certain populations.
Conversely, policy changes that expand rights, reduce stigma, or improve access to resources have been followed by measurable improvements in youth mental health (Raifman et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Conversely, policy changes that expand rights, reduce stigma, or improve access to resources have been followed by measurable improvements in youth mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Raifman et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: These effects highlight that macrosystem conditions are neither static nor inevitable but are actively constructed through political and societal choices.
Taken together, macrosystem processes define the structural and normative architecture within which adolescent development unfolds.

By producing patterned exposure to material hardship, discrimination, and normative pressure, the macrosystem sets the parameters for how risk is distributed and experienced across ecological systems.
These forces do not operate independently but are enacted through exosystem institutions and microsystem relationships, ultimately shaping individual vulnerability and resilience.

Understanding adolescent mental health therefore requires moving beyond individual-or family-level explanations to interrogate the social structures and cultural narratives that systematically generate distress.

Within the EEF-AMH, the chronosystem is reconceptualized not as a passive temporal backdrop but as an active developmental mechanism through which ecological risks accumulate, interact, and reorganize over time.

Development unfolds across multiple temporal scales-from daily routines and relational patterns to life-course transitions and sociohistorical events-and mental health vulnerability emerges through the timing, duration, and sequencing of exposures rather than through isolated stressors.
A process-oriented chronosystem perspective therefore emphasizes when, for how long, and in what combination ecological stressors are experienced.

In Figure 1, the chronosystem appears above the four ecological levels, and the arrows on the left show historical change, institutional change, developmental change, and cumulative exposure reaching the macrosystem, exosystem, microsystem, and individual levels, respectively.

text.text: A central chronosystem process is cumulative exposure.

Extensive longitudinal research demonstrates that repeated or chronic exposure to adversity-such as persistent family conflict, sustained socioeconomic disadvantage, or ongoing discrimination-is more strongly associated with adolescent mental health problems than single or time-limited events (Björkenstam et al., 2015; Raviv et al., 2010).

text.text: Cumulative stress models show dose-response relationships, whereby the number and duration of stressors predict steeper increases in depression, anxiety, and behavioral problems across development (Humphreys et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Cumulative stress models show dose-response relationships, whereby the number and duration of stressors predict steeper increases in depression, anxiety, and behavioral problems across development <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Humphreys et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: From an ecological perspective, accumulation reflects the compounding of stress across systems: macrosystem inequalities generate repeated exosystem constraints, which destabilize microsystem relationships and progressively embed vulnerability at the individual level.
Over time, this accumulation may overwhelm regulatory capacities and contribute to entrenched psychopathology.
Developmental timing further shapes how stress exposure translates into mental health outcomes.

Adolescence itself represents a period of heightened sensitivity due to pubertal maturation, ongoing brain development, and increasing reliance on peer and social evaluation (Jiang et al., 2021; Katsantonis, 2024; Kretzer et al., 2024).

text.text: Evidence indicates that exposure to adversity during early and mid-adolescence is particularly predictive of internalizing symptoms, as stress during these windows coincides with heightened emotional reactivity and stilldeveloping regulatory systems (McLaughlin et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Evidence indicates that exposure to adversity during early and mid-adolescence is particularly predictive of internalizing symptoms, as stress during these windows coincides with heightened emotional reactivity and stilldeveloping regulatory systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(McLaughlin et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Pubertal timing relative to peers further modifies risk, with early or off-time maturation associated with greater vulnerability to depression and anxiety (Stumper & Alloy, 2023).
text.formatted: Pubertal timing relative to peers further modifies risk, with early or off-time maturation associated with greater vulnerability to depression and anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">(Stumper & Alloy, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These findings underscore that associations between stressors and mental health are not uniform across development; rather, they depend critically on when stressors occur.
Normative developmental transitions constitute another chronosystem pathway linking ecological stress to mental health.

Transitions such as moving from primary to secondary school, changing peer networks, or entering late adolescence introduce periods of uncertainty and role redefinition that can temporarily heighten vulnerability (Evans et al., 2018; Lester et al., 2013; Sundqvist et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Transitions such as moving from primary to secondary school, changing peer networks, or entering late adolescence introduce periods of uncertainty and role redefinition that can temporarily heighten vulnerability <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Evans et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Lester et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Sundqvist et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: When transitions coincide with other stressors-such as family disruption, residential instability, or academic pressure-their psychological impact is amplified (Forehand et al., 1998; Henkens et al., 2024; Simsek et al., 2021).
text.formatted: When transitions coincide with other stressors-such as family disruption, residential instability, or academic pressure-their psychological impact is amplified <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Forehand et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Henkens et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Simsek et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, transitions can also represent opportunities for recalibration, particularly when accompanied by supportive microsystem relationships and adequate institutional resources (Neal et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Conversely, transitions can also represent opportunities for recalibration, particularly when accompanied by supportive microsystem relationships and adequate institutional resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Neal et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The chronosystem thus highlights how risk and resilience are dynamically shaped at points of developmental reorganization.
Beyond individual development, the chronosystem encompasses historical and cohortlevel contexts that shape the lives of entire generations of adolescents.
Large-scale sociohistorical events-such as economic recessions, pandemics, technological shifts, or climate change-alter the ecological landscape in which development unfolds.

The COVID-19 pandemic provides a clear illustration: widespread school closures, social isolation, and economic insecurity produced abrupt disruptions across microsystem and exosystem contexts, coinciding with marked increases in depressive and anxiety symptoms among adolescents worldwide (Madigan et al., 2023; Racine et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The COVID-19 pandemic provides a clear illustration: widespread school closures, social isolation, and economic insecurity produced abrupt disruptions across microsystem and exosystem contexts, coinciding with marked increases in depressive and anxiety symptoms among adolescents worldwide <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Madigan et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Racine et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Such events illustrate how macrosystem shocks may propagate through ecological systems, with possible lasting consequences for developmental trajectories.
Long-term global trends, including climate change and the rapid expansion of digital technologies, further exemplify chronosystem influences.

Climate-related anxiety reflects not only immediate environmental threats but also prolonged exposure to narratives of uncertainty and perceived lack of control over the future (Vercammen et al., 2025; Vergunst & Berry, 2021; Walinski et al., 2023).

text.text: Similarly, cohort-level increases in digital media use represent a temporal shift in the social ecology of adolescence, with implications for sleep, peer interaction, identity development, and emotional regulation (Crone & Konijn, 2018).

text.text: These trends show that adolescents are embedded not only in personal histories but also in evolving sociohistorical contexts that shape collective vulnerability.
Policy changes constitute another chronosystem mechanism that may be associated with changes in mental health trajectories at scale.

Shifts in laws, rights, and institutional protections -such as expansions or restrictions of healthcare access, educational reform, or changes in antidiscrimination policy-can function as turning points that either alleviate or exacerbate stress exposure for specific groups.

Evidence that reductions in structural stigma following policy reform are associated with improved mental health outcomes among marginalized youth highlights the temporal malleability of macrosystem conditions and their downstream effects (Raifman et al., 2017).

text.text: Taken together, the chronosystem captures the temporal architecture of risk, emphasizing that adolescent mental health is shaped by the accumulation, timing, and historical structuring of ecological stressors.

By foregrounding time as an explanatory dimension, the EEF-AMH clarifies why similar exposures may yield divergent outcomes across individuals and cohorts and why prevention efforts must be developmentally timed and historically informed.

Recognizing the chronosystem as an active process rather than a contextual backdrop completes a dynamic ecological account of adolescent mental health that integrates structure, relation, biology, and time.

This review proposes the Extended, Process-Oriented Ecological Framework for Adolescent Mental Health (EEF-AMH) as an extension of Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory and its later bioecological model.

Rather than treating ecological systems as discrete contexts in which correlates reside, the framework describes adolescent mental health vulnerability as the outcome of processes through which stress is produced, regulated, translated, embedded, and accumulated across systems and over time. to bottom, the central column traces the proposed cascade.
The macrosystem is the level of structural risk production, where socioeconomic inequality, discrimination and norms, policy environments, and digital culture shape patterned exposure to stress.
The exosystem regulates the resources that reach families and schools through educational governance, health care access, digital platforms, and community infrastructure.

The microsystem translates these pressures into daily emotional experience through family dynamics, peer relationships, school climate, and neighborhood context, and the label buffer/amplify indicates that this translation can weaken or strengthen the stress that arrives from above.

At the Individual level, emotional reactivity, genetic liability, epigenetic modification, and lifestyle factors shape how strongly stress is amplified and biologically embedded before it is expressed as depression, anxiety, self-harm, suicidality, posttraumatic stress disorder, or addictive behaviors.
Read from left to right, the figure shows that every level is also open to change over time.

The chronosystem appears above the cascade, and the arrows on the left show historical change reaching the macrosystem, institutional change reaching the exosystem, developmental change reaching the microsystem, and cumulative exposure reaching the individual.
Taken as a whole, the figure expresses the central claim of the framework.
Vulnerability is proposed to arise from the passage of stress across levels and over time rather than from any single level considered alone.
The primary theoretical contribution of the EEF-AMH lies in reframing ecological systems as mechanistic pathways rather than descriptive levels.

Traditional ecological applications often emphasize where risk factors are located-at the individual, family, school, or societal level-without specifying how these influences interact to shape developmental trajectories.
In contrast, the EEF-AMH articulates a set of interlocking processes through which distal structural conditions become proximal psychological vulnerabilities.

First, the framework foregrounds structural risk production at the macrosystem level, emphasizing that socioeconomic inequality, structural discrimination, cultural norms, and policy environments systematically generate patterned exposure to adversity.
These forces are not distal background conditions but foundational determinants that shape the distribution of risk across populations.
Second, the EEF-AMH conceptualizes the exosystem as a regulatory and distributive layer.

Institutional structures-such as healthcare systems, educational governance, community infrastructure, and digital platform regulation-influence whether families, schools, and peer networks are resourced to buffer stress or are instead left to absorb it.
This regulatory perspective highlights how mental health risk is shaped not only by exposure to stressors but also by the availability of institutional protection and support.
Third, the framework positions the microsystem as a translational nexus, where structural and institutional pressures are rendered psychologically meaningful through daily relational exchanges.
Family emotional climate, attachment security, peer belonging, and school connectedness emerge as key mechanisms through which ecological stressors are either buffered or amplified.
This reconceptualization moves beyond treating family or peer factors as independent predictors, instead situating them as mediators of broader ecological processes.
Fourth, at the person level, the EEF-AMH integrates biological embedding as a central explanatory process.

Genetic liability, emotional reactivity, and stress-related physiological changes are conceptualized not as isolated individual differences but as pathways through which cumulative ecological stress becomes internalized.
This integration bridges ecological theory with developmental psychopathology, clarifying how social conditions "get under the skin" to shape mental health risk.
Finally, the chronosystem is reconceptualized as an active temporal mechanism.

By emphasizing accumulation, sensitive periods, developmental transitions, and historical context, the EEF-AMH offers an account of why similar exposures may yield different outcomes depending on timing, duration, and cohort.

This temporal perspective is essential for understanding rising mental health difficulties among contemporary adolescents and for identifying developmentally timed points of intervention (Kirkbride et al., 2024).

text.text: Collectively, these contributions position the EEF-AMH as a theory-extending model that shifts ecological thinking from static categorization to dynamic explanation.

Without such a process-oriented approach, research risks underestimating how structural inequality, institutional design, and historical change interact to produce persistent mental health disparities.
The sections above describe each level separately, but the framework's central claim concerns how the levels connect.
A single example illustrates the proposed sequence.
Consider an economic recession that raises unemployment and household financial strain, an instance of structural risk production.
Its consequences at the exosystem level depend on institutional resources.

Where youth mental health services are scarce, costly, or slow to access, families and schools must manage emerging difficulties with little professional support (Graves et al., 2024; Radez et al., 2021).

Strain that begins in early adolescence coincides with a period of heightened neural and emotional sensitivity (McLaughlin et al., 2019), and strain that persists accumulates across years (Björkenstam et al., 2015).

In a natural experiment, families who moved out of poverty after receiving income supplements from a casino on tribal land saw their children's behavioral symptoms decline to the level of never-poor children, whereas children in persistently poor families showed no such change (Costello et al., 2003).

text.text: Exploratory analyses pointed to parental supervision as one family process through which the change in income may have operated.
Anxiety and depressive symptoms did not change, which suggests that different outcomes may depend on different links in the cascade.
This example is offered to illustrate the proposed sequence, not as evidence that every link has been tested together.
Studies that measure policy change, institutional resources, family processes, biological stress markers, and later symptoms within the same cohort are needed to test such cascades directly.
The EEF-AMH draws on several established frameworks that already integrate biological, developmental, and ecological perspectives.
Table 1 summarizes how it relates to each.
