text.text: The aim is not to replace these frameworks but to specify where the EEF-AMH extends them.
The bioecological model is the closest precursor.
It already places process at the center of development, includes characteristics of the person, and treats historical time as part of the chronosystem (Bronfenbrenner & Morris, 2006).
text.formatted: It already places process at the center of development, includes characteristics of the person, and treats historical time as part of the chronosystem <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Bronfenbrenner & Morris, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: The EEF-AMH retains these commitments but differs in what it treats as the core process.
The bioecological model centers on proximal processes as engines of competence and development, with the wider context acting mainly as a moderator of those processes.
The EEF-AMH centers on the transmission of stress and asks how risk generated at the top of the ecological hierarchy is regulated, translated, and embedded on its way to the adolescent.

It also assigns each level a distinct function rather than treating the outer levels as background conditions, and it specifies the biological mechanisms through which stress is embedded rather than describing the person through general characteristics.
Developmental psychopathology provides the framework's account of the person.

Its principles that pathways to disorder are probabilistic, that similar risks can lead to different outcomes, and that different risks can lead to similar outcomes are central to the EEF-AMH (Cicchetti & Rogosch, 2002).
text.formatted: Its principles that pathways to disorder are probabilistic, that similar risks can lead to different outcomes, and that different risks can lead to similar outcomes are central to the EEF-AMH <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Cicchetti & Rogosch, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Developmental psychopathology, however, is a broad perspective rather than a specified model of context.
The EEF-AMH adds an explicit account of where adversity originates and how it is distributed across adolescents before it reaches the person.

Biological embedding models propose how experience may become associated with persistent changes in stress physiology, gene regulation, and developmental biology (Danese & McEwen, 2012; Hertzman, 2012).
text.formatted: Biological embedding models propose how experience may become associated with persistent changes in stress physiology, gene regulation, and developmental biology <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Danese & McEwen, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Hertzman, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: These models supply the framework's person-level process.
Much of the foundational work on biological embedding has centered on early childhood (Hertzman, 2012).
text.formatted: Much of the foundational work on biological embedding has centered on early childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Hertzman, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The EEF-AMH applies these ideas to adolescence, when pubertal and neural change may create a further period of heightened sensitivity (Kretzer et al., 2024; McLaughlin et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The EEF-AMH applies these ideas to adolescence, when pubertal and neural change may create a further period of heightened sensitivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Kretzer et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">McLaughlin et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: It also places biological embedding at the end of a cross-level sequence and treats the microsystem and exosystem as points at which embedding may be interrupted.
Ecosocial theory is the closest population-level counterpart.

It proposes that people literally embody the material and social conditions in which they live, and that population patterns of disease reflect pathways of embodiment that operate at multiple levels and over the life course (Krieger, 2001).
text.formatted: It proposes that people literally embody the material and social conditions in which they live, and that population patterns of disease reflect pathways of embodiment that operate at multiple levels and over the life course <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Krieger, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: The EEF-AMH shares this view but differs in scale and purpose.

Ecosocial theory is an epidemiological theory for explaining the distribution of disease across populations, whereas the EEF-AMH is a developmental framework for explaining how vulnerability builds within individual adolescents.

It therefore gives more weight to relational processes in families and peer groups, to sensitive periods in adolescence, and to institutions such as schools and digital platforms that are specific to adolescent life.

Social determinants of health frameworks distinguish structural determinants, such as social position and policy, from intermediary determinants, such as material circumstances, psychosocial factors, and health systems (Kirkbride et al., 2024; Solar & Irwin, 2010).
text.formatted: Social determinants of health frameworks distinguish structural determinants, such as social position and policy, from intermediary determinants, such as material circumstances, psychosocial factors, and health systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Kirkbride et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Solar & Irwin, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The EEF-AMH adopts this distinction in its macrosystem and exosystem.

Social determinants frameworks are designed mainly to guide policy and to describe determinants at the population level, and they do not specify the developmental and relational mechanisms through which determinants reach an individual adolescent.
The EEF-AMH adds this developmental and relational layer and thereby links upstream policy targets to the family, peer, and biological processes that those policies are expected to change.
Taken together, the contribution of the EEF-AMH is integrative.
Each framework explains part of the pathway from social structure to adolescent mental health.
The EEF-AMH connects these parts into a single sequence with a named process at each ecological level and with time as a dimension that runs through all of them.
The EEF-AMH offers several implications for future research.
Empirically, the framework encourages multilevel and longitudinal designs capable of testing cross-system interactions and temporal dynamics.
Integrating biological markers with assessments of family processes, institutional context, and structural conditions may clarify pathways of cumulative risk.
Analytic approaches that model interaction, mediation, and accumulation-rather than isolated main effects-are particularly well suited to testing the framework's propositions.

For example, the framework predicts that associations between structural disadvantage and adolescent symptoms will be partly accounted for by institutional resources and family processes, and that these indirect associations will be stronger when exposure begins in early adolescence or persists over time.
For clinical and educational practice, the model underscores the limitations of interventions that focus exclusively on individual symptoms.
Screening and intervention efforts may be strengthened by assessing relational climate, institutional constraints, and chronic stress exposure alongside individual vulnerability.

Multilevel approaches-combining individual therapy, family-based interventions, school climate initiatives, and community support-are more consistent with the ecological processes identified in this review (Das et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Multilevel approaches-combining individual therapy, family-based interventions, school climate initiatives, and community support-are more consistent with the ecological processes identified in this review <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Das et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: At the policy level, the EEF-AMH highlights the importance of upstream prevention.

Policies that reduce socioeconomic inequality, expand access to mental health services, regulate digital environments, and counter structural discrimination have the potential to reduce stress exposure before it is translated into relational strain or biologically embedded vulnerability.
From this perspective, adolescent mental health is not solely a clinical issue but a matter of social design and governance.
Several limitations warrant consideration.
As a theory-extending narrative review, the EEF-AMH synthesizes evidence from diverse methodologies, many of which are correlational.
Although longitudinal and meta-analytic findings support proposed pathways, causal inference remains limited.
The literature reviewed was selected to illustrate the proposed processes and is not exhaustive.

The EEF-AMH should therefore be regarded as a conceptual synthesis rather than a formally validated theoretical model, and its propositions, including the ordering of processes shown in Figure 1, remain to be tested.
text.formatted: The EEF-AMH should therefore be regarded as a conceptual synthesis rather than a formally validated theoretical model, and its propositions, including the ordering of processes shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, remain to be tested.

text.text: Experimental and quasi-experimental studies-particularly those leveraging policy changes or natural experiments-will be critical for testing specific mechanisms within the framework.
The framework also emphasizes top-down transmission for clarity.

Adolescents' own characteristics and behavior shape their relationships and the contexts they select, consistent with the bioecological view of the person as an active agent in development (Bronfenbrenner & Morris, 2006), and these bottom-up influences deserve fuller treatment in future work.
text.formatted: Adolescents' own characteristics and behavior shape their relationships and the contexts they select, consistent with the bioecological view of the person as an active agent in development <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Bronfenbrenner & Morris, 2006)</ref>, and these bottom-up influences deserve fuller treatment in future work.

text.text: Additionally, much of the existing evidence is drawn from high-income, Western contexts, which may limit generalizability.
Cultural variability in family structure, institutional arrangements, and normative expectations suggests the need for cross-cultural validation and adaptation of the framework.
Finally, rapid technological and social change means that ecological conditions will continue to evolve, requiring ongoing refinement of theoretical models to remain relevant.
The EEF-AMH offers a contemporary, process-oriented account of how individual vulnerability and environmental context jointly shape adolescent mental health.

By integrating structural risk production, institutional regulation, relational translation, biological embedding, and temporal accumulation within a unified ecological model, the framework advances theoretical understanding and provides a foundation for more equitable, developmentally informed approaches to prevention and intervention.
Addressing adolescent mental health therefore requires not only supporting individuals and families, but also reshaping the ecological systems and historical conditions in which development unfolds.
(EEF-AMH).
The EEF-AMH describes how stress is produced, regulated, translated, biologically embedded, and accumulated across ecological systems during adolescence.
The central column shows four ecological levels, each with its proposed process and examples of relevant factors.
The macrosystem is the level of structural production of risk (socioeconomic inequality, discrimination and norms, policy environments, and digital culture and media).
The exosystem provides institutional regulation of resources (educational governance, health care access, digital platforms, and community infrastructure).
The microsystem is the site of relational translation and emotional climate (family dynamics, peer relationships, school climate, and neighborhood context).
The Individual level represents biological sensitivity and embedding (emotional reactivity, genetic liability, epigenetic modification, and lifestyle factors).

Arrows on the right indicate the proposed downward transmission of stress and are labeled with the process at each step (risk production, resource regulation, relational translation, and stress amplification).
The label buffer/amplify indicates that microsystem processes can weaken or strengthen stress arriving from higher levels.
The final arrow leads to mental health outcomes (depression, anxiety, self-harm, suicidality, posttraumatic stress disorder [PTSD], and addictive behaviors).
The chronosystem, shown at the top, represents temporal dynamics across systems (sensitive periods, cumulative stress, life transitions, and historical events).

Arrows on the left indicate that temporal change reaches every level, as historical change (macrosystem), institutional change (exosystem), developmental change (microsystem), and cumulative exposure (individual).
All arrows represent hypothesized pathways rather than established causal effects.
